feedback: A full response judges irreversibility by new-substance evidence (gas, colour, heat/light, new solid), rules out mixing or boiling, and transfers the signs to burning and rusting.

A partial response names 'new substance / can't get it back' plus one sign (fizzing) but cannot yet marshal the full set or transfer to other cases — acknowledge the case recognised and prompt for a second sign and a new example.

A gap response says it can't be undone with no sign, or reads fizzing as boiling/mixing — reteach using the sand+salt separable-mixture contrast and the no-heating point (cold ingredients still made gas).
activities.intendedInsight: A gas appearing with no heating is strong evidence of a newly-made substance, which distinguishes an irreversible chemical change from mere mixing or boiling.
learnerActions: Before mixing, predict what a balloon stretched over a bottle containing a little baking soda will do when vinegar is tipped in — and say WHY.
Tip in the vinegar, observe the balloon inflate, and explain what the gas tells you about whether a new substance was made.

Answer probing questions: burning toast, a firework, and rusting iron — what sign in each shows a new substance formed? If nothing was heated, why did a gas appear? How is this different from stirring sand into salt, which you CAN separate again? If someone says 'it's just hidden, not changed', what evidence shows it is really new?
activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: the balloon and the bottle

feedback: If a change is sorted correctly but the justifying sign is missing or wrong, ask which specific sign was observed.
If a mixture (sand+salt) is called irreversible, point to its separability — no new substance was made.
Reinforce when a learner pairs each irreversible case with a distinct, correct sign.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying a change requires justification by an observed sign, not just a label — and a separable mixture is not an irreversible change.
learnerActions: Sort a set of changes into reversible and irreversible, explaining the reason for each.

For each irreversible change, match it to the evidence-of-new-substance sign that justifies the classification (e.g. acid+bicarb → gas produced; rusting → new solid / colour change; burning → heat/light given off + ash as a new solid).
Contrast a genuine mixture (sand stirred into salt, separable) with a change that made a new substance, and state why one can be undone and the other cannot.
activities.title: Sort and match: reversible vs irreversible by its sign
